vaisakhi.s: Vaisakhi, or Baisakhi, is a spring harvest festival of the Punjab and one of the most important festivals of the Sikh calendar, commemorating the founding of the Khalsa. In 1801, on the day of Vaisakhi, Ranjit Singh was proclaimed Maharaja of the Punjab at Lahore.

vaishali.s: Vaishali was an ancient city in the north of present-day Bihar in eastern India, associated with the early Buddhist and Jain traditions. In the Gupta period it was an important urban centre.

vakil.s: Vakil was a Persian title meaning deputy or regent, used for a high office of state in Safavid Iran. The Zand ruler Karim Khan adopted it rather than the title of Shah, presenting himself as regent rather than king.

vakil-al-ruaya.s: Vakil al-Ruaya, meaning Regent of the People, was the title adopted by Karim Khan, founder of the Zand Empire. The Zand Empire profile explains that he refused to take the title of Shah.

vakil-bath.s: The Vakil Bath is a historic public bathhouse in Shiraz, Iran, built under Karim Khan during the Zand period. It forms part of the architectural ensemble with which he adorned his capital.

vakil-bazaar.s: The Vakil Bazaar is the main covered market of Shiraz, Iran, built under Karim Khan during the Zand period. Its vaulted brick arcades formed the commercial heart of the Zand capital.

vakil-mosque.s: The Vakil Mosque is a mosque in Shiraz, Iran, built under Karim Khan during the Zand period, next to the Vakil Bazaar. It is noted for its prayer hall of carved stone columns and its tile decoration.

valencia.s: Valencia is a city on the Mediterranean coast of eastern Spain, surrounded by a fertile irrigated plain known as the huerta. In the medieval period it was an important city of al-Andalus.

valens.s: Valens was Roman emperor in the east from 364 until his death in 378 CE. He allowed Gothic refugees to cross the Danube into the empire, but their mistreatment led to revolt.

valerian.s: Valerian was a Roman emperor of the mid-third century CE who campaigned against the Sasanian Empire. In 260 CE he was captured by the Sasanian king Shapur I after the Battle of Edessa, becoming the first Roman emperor taken prisoner by a foreign enemy.

valladolid-debate.s: The Valladolid debate was a formal dispute held in Spain in 1550–1551 on the treatment of the indigenous peoples of the Americas. Bartolomé de las Casas defended their rights and humanity, while Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda argued that their conquest and subjugation were justified.

valley-of-mexico.s: The Valley of Mexico is a highland basin in central Mexico that once contained a system of shallow lakes, including Lake Texcoco. It was densely populated and home to many city-states.

vandal-conquest-of-north-africa.s: The Vandal conquest of North Africa was the seizure of Roman Africa by the Vandals and Alans between 429 and 439 CE. Crossing from Spain under King Gaiseric, they captured Carthage in 439 and established a kingdom that controlled much of the western Mediterranean.

vandals.s: The Vandals were a Germanic people who migrated through Gaul and Spain before crossing into North Africa in 429 CE. They established a kingdom centred on Carthage and sacked Rome in 455 CE.

vanuatu.s: Vanuatu is an island nation in the south-western Pacific Ocean, formerly known as the New Hebrides. It was governed as an Anglo-French condominium.

varna.s: Varna is the classical Indian system dividing society into four broad orders: Brahmins (priests), Kshatriyas (warriors and rulers), Vaishyas (merchants and farmers) and Shudras (labourers and servants). It was set out in Sanskrit religious and legal texts.

vasco-da-gama.s: Vasco da Gama was a Portuguese navigator who led the first European voyage to reach India by sea, arriving at Calicut in 1498 after rounding the Cape of Good Hope. His voyage opened a direct maritime route between Europe and Asia.

vassal.s: A vassal is a ruler or lord who holds power or land in subordination to a superior, owing loyalty, tribute or military service in return for protection or recognition. Vassalage was a widespread means of extending imperial authority without direct administration.

vassal-and-tributary-systems.s: Vassal and tributary systems describe the recurring pattern by which empires ruled indirectly through subordinate rulers who kept local authority in exchange for tribute, military service and acknowledgement of overlordship. Such systems allowed rapid expansion at low cost but…

vastryoshan.s: The vastryoshan were the commoners in the social hierarchy of the Sasanian Empire, comprising both peasant cultivators and artisans. The Sasanian Empire profile explains that society was divided into four estates: priests, warriors, scribes and administrators, and commoners.

venetia.s: Venetia is a historical region of north-eastern Italy centred on Venice. After the Napoleonic Wars it was ruled by the Austrian Empire as part of the Kingdom of Lombardy–Venetia.

venice.s: Venice is a city in north-eastern Italy built on islands in a lagoon, which became a major maritime and commercial republic in the medieval period. Venetian merchants gained extensive trading privileges in the Byzantine Empire from 1082, and Venice played a leading role in the…

verden.s: Verden is a town in Lower Saxony, northern Germany, historically the seat of a prince-bishopric. Under the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, Sweden received the bishoprics of Bremen and Verden, together with Wismar and western Pomerania.

versailles.s: Versailles is a town near Paris and the site of the vast palace built by Louis XIV, which became the seat of the French court and a symbol of absolute monarchy. In 1871 the German Empire was proclaimed in its Hall of Mirrors after the defeat of France.

viceroy-of-india.s: A viceroy is an official who governs a country or province in the name of a monarch. The title is best known for the Viceroy of India, the head of British government in India after 1858, who governed the Raj with the Indian Civil Service.

viceroy-of-kush.s: The Viceroy of Kush, also called the King's Son of Kush, was the official who governed Nubia on behalf of the pharaoh during Egypt's New Kingdom. The Egyptian Empire New Kingdom profile describes the office as a semi-autonomous imperial sub-administration.

viceroy-of-portuguese-india.s: The Viceroy of Portuguese India was the governor of the Estado da Índia, the Portuguese colonial administration in Asia, based at Goa from the early sixteenth century. The Portuguese Empire profile notes that his authority nominally extended over all Portuguese possessions…

viceroyalty-of-new-spain.s: The Viceroyalty of New Spain was the administrative unit of the Spanish Empire covering Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, parts of what is now the United States and later the Philippines. It was established in 1535 with its capital at Mexico City.

viceroyalty-of-peru.s: The Viceroyalty of Peru was the administrative unit of the Spanish Empire created in 1542 to govern most of Spanish South America, with its capital at Lima. Its silver mines, especially Potosí, made it a principal source of imperial revenue.

victory-stele-of-naram-sin.s: The Victory Stele of Naram-Sin is a carved stone monument celebrating the Akkadian king Naram-Sin's victory over the Lullubi mountain people, showing the king ascending a mountain above his defeated enemies. It is a masterpiece of Akkadian art.

vienna.s: Vienna is the capital of Austria, on the Danube, and was for centuries the seat of the Habsburg monarchy. It withstood Ottoman sieges in 1529 and 1683, the second of which was broken with the help of a Polish-Lithuanian relief army under Jan III Sobieski.

vienna-secession.s: The Vienna Secession was an art movement founded in 1897 by Gustav Klimt and other artists who broke away from Vienna's established academic art association. It promoted modern styles in painting, architecture and design.

viet-minh.s: The Viet Minh was a Vietnamese independence movement founded in 1941 under the leadership of Ho Chi Minh. It fought against Japanese occupation and then against the restoration of French colonial rule in the First Indochina War.

vietnam.s: Vietnam is a country in mainland Southeast Asia along the eastern coast of the Indochinese peninsula. Its northern part was long under Chinese rule, including periods of Han and Tang administration, and it absorbed Confucian governance traditions.

vijayanagara-empire.s: The Vijayanagara Empire was a powerful Hindu state in southern India founded around 1336, with its capital at Vijayanagara on the Tungabhadra River. It arose as Delhi Sultanate control over the Deccan and the south weakened.

vikings.s: The Vikings were seafaring Scandinavians who raided, traded and settled across Europe from the late eighth to the eleventh centuries. Their raids devastated the coasts and river valleys of the divided Carolingian kingdoms, and the Carolingian Empire profile notes Charles the…

villa-estate.s: A villa, in the Carolingian context, was a great landed estate belonging to the church, the crown or the aristocracy. The Carolingian Empire profile describes these villae as the primary units of agricultural production and local governance.

virginia.s: Virginia is a region on the Atlantic coast of North America, named in honour of Queen Elizabeth I. The colony founded at Jamestown in 1607 was the first permanent English settlement in America.

vishaya.s: A vishaya was an administrative district in the Gupta Empire and other early Indian states. The Gupta Empire profile explains that the provinces, or bhuktis, governed by uparikas were subdivided into vishayas.

vishayapati.s: A vishayapati was the official in charge of a vishaya, or district, in the Gupta Empire. The Gupta Empire profile notes that vishayapatis were often drawn from local merchant guilds, working beneath the provincial governors known as uparikas.

vishnugupta.s: Vishnugupta was the last recognised emperor of the Gupta dynasty, ruling around 540–550 CE. By his time the empire had been reduced to a remnant kingdom by Huna invasions, succession disputes and the rise of regional powers.

visigoths.s: The Visigoths were a Gothic Germanic people who entered the Roman Empire in the late fourth century. They destroyed a Roman army and killed Emperor Valens at Adrianople in 378 CE, and under Alaric they sacked Rome in 410 CE.

vizier.s: A vizier is a high minister or chief administrator serving a ruler, a title used in many Islamic states and applied by historians to the chief officials of ancient Egypt. In the Abbasid Caliphate the vizier headed the bureaucracy, and the Seljuk vizier Nizam al-Mulk became the…

vo-nguyen-giap.s: Vo Nguyen Giap was a Vietnamese military commander, the principal general of the Viet Minh and later of North Vietnam. He led the Viet Minh forces in the First Indochina War against France.

volga.s: The Volga is the longest river in Europe, flowing through central Russia to the Caspian Sea. It was a major artery of trade linking the Baltic and northern forests with the Caspian, Central Asia and the Islamic world.

volga-trade-route.s: The Volga trade route was a network of river and portage routes linking Scandinavia and the Baltic with the Caspian Sea and the Islamic world via the Volga River in the early medieval period. Furs, slaves and other goods moved south, while silver dirhams flowed north.

volhynia.s: Volhynia is a historical region in north-western Ukraine. It formed part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania until 1569.

volta-river.s: The Volta is a river system of West Africa that flows south through present-day Ghana to the Gulf of Guinea. The Oyo Empire profile notes that around 1748, at the height of Oyo power, its tributary network stretched from the Niger River in the east to the Volta corridor in the…

voorcompagnieen.s: The voorcompagnieën, or pre-companies, were the Dutch trading companies formed in the 1590s to send ships to Asia before the creation of the Dutch East India Company. Their competition drove up prices in Asia and lowered profits in Europe.

viet-cong.s: The Viet Cong, formally the National Liberation Front for South Vietnam, was the communist-led political and military organisation founded in 1960 to overthrow the government of the Republic of Vietnam. Backed by North Vietnam, it waged guerrilla war throughout the Vietnam War…

viking-age.s: The Viking Age is the period from the late 8th to the mid 11th century in which Scandinavians raided, traded and settled across Europe and the North Atlantic. Its beginning is usually dated to the raid on Lindisfarne in 793 and its end to 1066.

vincent-of-saragossa.s: Vincent of Saragossa was a deacon of Zaragoza who was martyred at Valencia in the persecution of Diocletian, around 304. He became one of the most widely venerated saints of Spain.

vir-singh-deo.s: Vir Singh Deo, also written Bir Singh Deo, was the Bundela Rajput ruler of Orchha from 1605 to 1627. In 1602 he had Akbar's minister Abul Fazl killed at the request of Prince Salim, and when Salim became the emperor Jahangir he rewarded him with Orchha and high Mughal rank.

vladimir-ii-monomakh.s: Vladimir Monomakh was Prince of Pereyaslavl and Chernigov and, from 1113, Grand Prince of Kiev. A grandson of Yaroslav the Wise and, through his mother, of the Byzantine emperor Constantine IX Monomachos, he led repeated campaigns against the Cumans and took part in the…

victor-emmanuel-iii.s: Victor Emmanuel III was King of Italy from 1900 to 1946. He appointed Benito Mussolini prime minister in 1922 and accepted the titles Emperor of Ethiopia in 1936 and King of the Albanians in 1939 after Italian conquests.

victor-emmanuel-ii.s: Victor Emmanuel II was King of Sardinia from 1849 and the first King of Italy from 1861. With his prime minister Cavour he allied with France against Austria in 1859, ceding Savoy and Nice to France in 1860, and annexed most of the peninsula.

volunteer-army.s: The Volunteer Army was the main anti-Bolshevik White army in southern Russia during the Russian Civil War, formed in late 1917 by generals Mikhail Alekseyev and Lavr Kornilov and later led by Anton Denikin. Based in the Kuban and North Caucasus, it fought the Red Army and…

vasily-ii-of-moscow.s: Vasily II was grand prince of Moscow from 1425 to 1462. His reign was dominated by a long civil war with his uncle Yuri of Galich and Yuri's sons; in 1446 Dmitry Shemyaka and Ivan of Mozhaysk captured and blinded him.

vasily-iii-of-moscow.s: Vasily III was grand prince of Moscow from 1505 to 1533, son of Ivan III and father of Ivan the Terrible. He completed the gathering of the Russian lands, ending the independence of Pskov in 1510, taking Smolensk from Lithuania in 1514 and annexing Ryazan in 1521.

vere-bird.s: Vere Cornwall Bird was a trade unionist and politician who led Antigua from the 1950s. As chief minister and then premier of the self-governing colony, and from independence in 1981 the first prime minister of Antigua and Barbuda, he dominated politics until 1994, when his son…

victor-amadeus-ii.s: Victor Amadeus II was duke of Savoy from 1675. Changing sides skilfully in the wars of Louis XIV, he gained Sicily and a royal title by the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713, exchanging it for Sardinia in 1720.

viracocha-inca.s: Viracocha Inca was the eighth ruler of the Kingdom of Cusco in Inca tradition. He extended Cusco's power over neighbouring valleys and allied with the Lupaca of Lake Titicaca.

vladimir-lenin.s: Vladimir Lenin was a Russian revolutionary who led the Bolshevik party. He organised the October Revolution of 1917, headed the government of Soviet Russia through the Civil War and founded the Soviet Union in 1922.

vsevolod-the-big-nest.s: Vsevolod III, called the Big Nest for his many sons, was grand prince of Vladimir-Suzdal from 1176 to 1212. He made Vladimir the strongest principality of north-eastern Rus' and dominated Novgorod and Ryazan.

vercingetorix.s: Vercingetorix was a chief of the Arverni who in 52 BCE united most of the Gauls in revolt against Julius Caesar. He used scorched-earth tactics and repulsed Caesar at Gergovia, but was besieged at Alesia, the town of the Mandubii, and surrendered when a relief army failed.

vajrayana.s: Vajrayana, or Tantric Buddhism, is a form of Mahayana Buddhism that developed in India from around the 7th century, using ritual, mantras, mandalas and initiation by a teacher to seek rapid enlightenment. It spread to Tibet, East Asia and maritime South-East Asia, where…

vakpati-munja.s: Vakpati Munja was a king of the Paramara dynasty of Malwa in central India in the late 10th century. A poet and patron of scholars, he raided neighbouring kingdoms, including the Kalachuris, Guhilas and Chahamanas, and fought repeatedly against Tailapa II of the Western…

val-di-chiana.s: The Val di Chiana is a broad valley in eastern Tuscany and western Umbria, running from near Arezzo south to Chiusi and Lake Trasimeno. In Etruscan times its fertile soils supported Clusium, Cortona and Arretium and linked central Etruria with the Tiber and Arno valleys.

valdemar-iv-of-denmark.s: Valdemar IV, known as Valdemar Atterdag, was King of Denmark from 1340 to 1375 and rebuilt the kingdom after years in which its provinces had been pawned to foreign lords, recovering Zealand, Scania and other lands. In 1361 he invaded Gotland and took Visby, provoking war with…

vasyl-chuchupak.s: Vasyl Chuchupak was a Ukrainian insurgent leader who in 1919 organised a peasant self-defence force around the Motronynskyi Monastery in the Kholodny Yar forest of central Ukraine. Declaring loyalty to the Ukrainian People's Republic, the Kholodny Yar Republic controlled some…

via-aemilia.s: The Via Aemilia was a Roman road built in 187 BCE by the consul Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, running in a straight line along the northern edge of the Apennines from Ariminum (Rimini) to Placentia (Piacenza) on the Po. Towns along it, including Bologna, Modena, Reggio and Parma,…

via-francigena.s: The Via Francigena was the main medieval road and pilgrim route from France and northern Europe across the Alps to Rome, described in the itinerary of Archbishop Sigeric of Canterbury around 990. In Tuscany it passed through Lucca, San Gimignano and Siena, whose trade, inns…

vicente-guerrero.s: Vicente Guerrero was a leader of the Mexican War of Independence who kept up guerrilla resistance in the south after 1815. In 1821 he joined the royalist officer Agustín de Iturbide in the Plan of Iguala, which brought independence.

victor-hugues.s: Victor Hugues was a French revolutionary commissioner who in 1794 recaptured Guadeloupe from the British and enforced the National Convention's abolition of slavery there, while executing royalists and sending privateers against enemy shipping. As governor of French Guiana…

vigraharaja-iv.s: Vigraharaja IV was a king of the Chahamanas of Shakambhari in Rajasthan in the mid-12th century who expanded the kingdom north by taking Delhi from the Tomara dynasty, whose chiefs continued as his vassals. A patron of learning, he wrote the Sanskrit play Harakeli Nataka,…

vladislaus-iii-duke-of-bohemia.s: Vladislaus Henry, a Přemyslid prince, was briefly Duke of Bohemia in 1197 as Vladislaus III before giving up the throne to his brother Ottokar I in return for Moravia. As Margrave of Moravia from 1197 until his death in 1222 he united the former Moravian appanages of Brno,…

volodymyr-olgerdovich.s: Volodymyr Olgerdovich was a son of Grand Duke Algirdas of Lithuania who ruled the Principality of Kiev as a Lithuanian prince from about 1362 to 1394. He minted his own coins and kept considerable independence until Vytautas removed him in 1395 and gave him Slutsk and Kapyl in…

vseslav-of-polotsk.s: Vseslav of Polotsk was prince of Polotsk from 1044 to 1101 and a rival of the sons of Yaroslav the Wise. Defeated on the Nemiga river near Minsk in 1067, he was seized during negotiations and imprisoned in Kiev, but the Kievans freed him in 1068 and briefly made him their prince.

vuk-brankovic.s: Vuk Branković was a Serbian noble, son-in-law of Prince Lazar, who after the break-up of the Serbian Empire built up a lordship in Kosovo and northern Macedonia rich in silver mines. He fought at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389 and was later, unjustly, cast in epic poetry as…

valdemar-i-of-denmark.s: Valdemar I, called the Great, was King of Denmark from 1157 to 1182, ending a long period of civil war. With his adviser Bishop Absalon he led repeated campaigns against the Wends of the southern Baltic coast.

vaballathus.s: Vaballathus was the son of Odaenathus and Zenobia of Palmyra, in whose name his mother ruled the Palmyrene Empire after his father's murder in 267. Under Zenobia's regency Palmyra took Egypt and much of Asia Minor, and in 272 Vaballathus was proclaimed Augustus.

vachagan-iii.s: Vachagan III, called the Pious, was king of Caucasian Albania in the late 5th and early 6th centuries, of the Arsacid line. Restored around 485 after a revolt against Sasanian attempts to impose Zoroastrianism, he promoted Christianity, built churches and around 488 summoned…

vaclav-havel.s: Václav Havel was a Czech playwright, dissident and statesman. A founder of the Charter 77 human rights movement, he was imprisoned several times by the communist regime.

vakhtang-vi-of-kartli.s: Vakhtang VI was king of Kartli in eastern Georgia, ruling as regent from 1703 and as king in 1716 and from 1719 to 1724 under Safavid overlordship. A scholar and lawgiver, he compiled a law code, organised the editing of the Georgian chronicles and set up the first printing…

valdemar-ii-of-denmark.s: Valdemar II, called the Victorious, was king of Denmark from 1202 to 1241. He extended Danish power along the southern Baltic and in 1219 led a crusade to northern Estonia, landing at Lindanise, where he built the castle that grew into Tallinn.

valentin-alsina.s: Valentín Alsina was an Argentine lawyer and politician, a leading figure of the State of Buenos Aires after its secession from the Argentine Confederation in 1852. As governor in 1852 and again from 1857 to 1859, he defended the province's control of its port revenues against…

vali-khan.s: Vali Khan was khan of the Kazakh Middle Juz from 1781 until his death in 1819, succeeding his father Ablai Khan. Recognised by both the Russian Empire and the Qing Empire, he struggled to control rival sultans, and Russia began to deal with other claimants, recognising a rival…

valley-of-oaxaca.s: The Valley of Oaxaca is a highland valley in southern Mexico, formed by three arms that meet at the modern city of Oaxaca. It was the heartland of Zapotec civilisation: early villages such as San José Mogote grew there, and around 500 BCE Monte Albán was founded on a hilltop…

vandad-hormozd.s: Vandad Hormozd was a ruler of the Qarinvand dynasty in the Alborz mountains of Tabaristan, northern Iran, in the late 8th century. In the 780s he led a revolt against the Abbasid Caliphate with the Bavandid ruler Sharwin, killing many Arab settlers and officials.

varaz-grigor.s: Varaz Grigor was the first prince of Caucasian Albania from the Mihranid dynasty, a branch of a great Parthian noble family that held the canton of Gardman. Around 630, as the Sasanian Empire fell into crisis, he became ruler of all Albania, governing from Partav, modern…

vasco-fernandes-coutinho.s: Vasco Fernandes Coutinho was a Portuguese nobleman, a veteran of service in India, who received the hereditary captaincy of Espírito Santo in Brazil from King John III in 1534. He landed in 1535 and founded Vila Velha, but attacks by the Goitacá and other peoples, quarrels…

vasco-nunez-de-balboa.s: Vasco Núñez de Balboa was a Spanish conquistador who in 1510 founded Santa María la Antigua del Darién, the first lasting Spanish settlement on the American mainland. In September 1513 he crossed the Isthmus of Panama and became the first European to see the Pacific from the…

vasilko-konstantinovich.s: Vasilko Konstantinovich was prince of Rostov from 1218 to 1238, the eldest son of Konstantin of Rostov. He fought with the forces of Vladimir-Suzdal against the Mongols at the Battle of the Sit River in March 1238 and was captured.

vasily-of-kostroma.s: Vasily of Kostroma was the youngest son of Grand Prince Yaroslav II of Vladimir and the first prince of Kostroma, which he received as his appanage after his father's death in 1246. He fought the Lithuanians and the Novgorodians, and in 1272 became grand prince of Vladimir…

vasily-shemyachich.s: Vasily Shemyachich was prince of Novgorod-Seversky and a grandson of Dmitry Shemyaka. In 1500 he transferred his allegiance and his lands from the Grand Duchy of Lithuania to Moscow, a gain confirmed by the truce of 1503.

vasily-yaroslavich-of-serpukhov.s: Vasily Yaroslavich was prince of Serpukhov and Borovsk, a grandson of Vladimir the Bold and brother-in-law of Grand Prince Vasily II of Moscow. During Moscow's dynastic civil war he loyally supported Vasily II against Dmitry Shemyaka.

vasishthiputra-chamtamula.s: Vasishthiputra Chamtamula, also known as Santamula I, was the founder of the Ikshvaku dynasty in the lower Krishna valley of Andhra in the early 3rd century, after the collapse of the Satavahana dynasty. He built the capital Vijayapuri in the valley now called Nagarjunakonda…

veera-ballala-ii.s: Veera Ballala II was king of the Hoysala Empire in southern India from 1173 to 1220. He declared full independence from the Western Chalukyas around 1187, defeated the Seuna Yadavas and made the Hoysalas the leading power of the southern Deccan, later intervening in the Tamil…

veera-ballala-iii.s: Veera Ballala III was the last major king of the Hoysala Empire, ruling from 1292 to 1343. Malik Kafur, general of Alauddin Khalji, sacked his capital Dwarasamudra in 1311 and forced him to pay tribute.

vela-jimenez.s: Vela Jiménez was count of Álava in the late 9th century, one of the frontier lords of the Kingdom of Asturias. The Asturian chronicles record him defending the castle of Cellorigo against the armies of the Emirate of Córdoba in 882 and 883. Álava was then a largely…

venta-belgarum.s: Venta Belgarum was the Roman town at Winchester in Hampshire, capital of the civitas of the Belgae in Roman Britain. It grew near a late Iron Age enclosure at Oram's Arbour and became one of the larger towns of the province, with a street grid, a forum and defensive walls.

venta-silurum.s: Venta Silurum was the Roman town at Caerwent in south-east Wales, capital of the civitas of the Silures after their conquest in the 70s CE. It had a forum, basilica, temples and baths, and later strong stone walls that still stand.

veronica-gambara.s: Veronica Gambara was an Italian Renaissance poet and stateswoman from Brescia. She married Giberto X, lord of Correggio, in 1509 and after his death in 1518 governed the small state for her sons, defending it during the Italian Wars.

vespasiano-gonzaga.s: Vespasiano Gonzaga was an Italian nobleman, soldier and patron from a cadet branch of the Gonzaga family, who served Philip II of Spain as a military engineer and as viceroy of Navarre and Valencia. From the 1550s he rebuilt his town of Sabbioneta, between Mantua and Parma, as…

vibhaji-ajoji.s: Vibhaji Ajoji was the founder of Rajkot State in the Kathiawar peninsula of western India. A Jadeja Rajput and grandson of Jam Sataji of Nawanagar, he received the area as his share of the family lands and founded the town of Rajkot in 1620.

vibhuti-narayan-singh.s: Vibhuti Narayan Singh was the last ruling Maharaja of Benares, succeeding in 1939 while still a boy. He acceded to the Indian Union after independence, and in 1949 Benares State was merged into Uttar Pradesh.

vibo-valentia.s: Vibo Valentia is a town in Calabria, southern Italy, on the site of Hipponion, a Greek colony founded by Locri Epizephyrii in the 7th century BCE. After a period under the Bruttians, it became the Latin colony of Vibo Valentia in 192 BCE and served as a port on the Tyrrhenian…

victor-paz-estenssoro.s: Víctor Paz Estenssoro was a Bolivian statesman who founded the Revolutionary Nationalist Movement (MNR) and served as president four times. Leading the 1952 revolution, he introduced universal suffrage, nationalised the tin mines and began land reform.

victor-schoelcher.s: Victor Schoelcher was a French politician and journalist who led the campaign to abolish slavery in the French colonies. As under-secretary for the colonies in the provisional government of the Second Republic, he drafted the decree of 27 April 1848 that abolished slavery…

vidkun-quisling.s: Vidkun Quisling was a Norwegian army officer and politician who founded the fascist party Nasjonal Samling in 1933. On 9 April 1940, the day Germany invaded Norway, he proclaimed himself head of government; the Germans soon set him aside, but in 1942 made him…

vieille-montagne.s: Vieille Montagne, in German Altenberg, was a zinc ore mine at Kelmis (La Calamine), between Aachen and Liège, worked since the Middle Ages for calamine used in brass-making. In 1816 the Netherlands and Prussia could not agree who should have it and left the surrounding area as…

vigdis-finnbogadottir.s: Vigdís Finnbogadóttir was president of Iceland from 1980 to 1996, the world's first woman elected head of state in a democratic national election. A teacher and director of the Reykjavík Theatre Company before her election, she was re-elected three times.

vijayabahu-i.s: Vijayabahu I was king of Sri Lanka from 1055 to 1110. Leading resistance from the southern Kingdom of Ruhuna against the Chola Empire, which had ruled northern Sri Lanka since the early 11th century, he drove out the Cholas and took Polonnaruwa in 1070, making it his capital.

vijayabahu-iii-of-dambadeniya.s: Vijayabahu III of Dambadeniya was a Sinhalese king who founded a new royal line after the fall of Polonnaruwa to the invader Kalinga Magha. He established himself at the rock fortress of Dambadeniya in the island's wet zone and recovered the Tooth Relic, making Dambadeniya the…

vijayaditya-iii.s: Vijayaditya III, also called Gunaga Vijayaditya, was the most warlike ruler of the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi. He fought the Rashtrakutas and their allies across the Deccan, and his inscriptions claim campaigns as far as the Ganges, raising the Vengi kingdom to the peak of its…

vijayaraghava-nayak.s: Vijayaraghava Nayak was the last Nayak ruler of Thanjavur in southern India, a patron of Telugu literature and music at his court. His long reign ended in war with Chokkanatha Nayak of Madurai, whose army took Thanjavur in 1673; Vijayaraghava was killed, and the kingdom soon…

vikramaditya-ii.s: Vikramaditya II was a king of the Chalukyas of Badami in the western Deccan. He defeated the Pallavas and occupied their capital Kanchipuram, where he spared the temples and made gifts to them, and his queens built the Virupaksha and Mallikarjuna temples at Pattadakal to mark…

vikramaditya-vi.s: Vikramaditya VI was the most celebrated ruler of the Western Chalukya Empire of Kalyani. During a fifty-year reign he founded the Chalukya Vikrama era, held off the Cholas and patronised scholars, among them the poet Bilhana, who wrote his biography, and the jurist…

viktor-chernov.s: Viktor Chernov was a founder and leading theorist of the Russian Socialist Revolutionary Party and minister of agriculture in the Provisional Government of 1917. In January 1918 he was elected chairman of the Russian Constituent Assembly, which the Bolsheviks dispersed after a…

viktor-orban.s: Viktor Orbán is a Hungarian politician, a founder of the Fidesz party in 1988 and prime minister from 1998 to 2002 and again from 2010. His government used its two-thirds parliamentary majority to adopt a new constitution, the Fundamental Law of 2011, and his long dominance…

vilmos-tkalecz.s: Vilmos Tkálecz was a Slovene-speaking teacher and politician from the Prekmurje region of Hungary. On 29 May 1919, during the turmoil of the Hungarian Soviet Republic, he proclaimed the independent Republic of Prekmurje, or Mura Republic, at Murska Sobota; it was crushed…

vimara-peres.s: Vímara Peres was a vassal of King Alfonso III of Asturias who took the town of Portucale, modern Porto, from the Moors in 868. He was made count of the land between the Minho and Douro rivers, founding the County of Portugal from which the later kingdom took its name.

vincas-mickevicius-kapsukas.s: Vincas Mickevičius-Kapsukas was a Lithuanian communist leader and writer. He headed the Soviet government of Lithuania in 1918–1919 and then chaired the council of people's commissars of the short-lived Lithuanian–Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic, before working for the…

vincent-auriol.s: Vincent Auriol was a French Socialist politician and the first President of the French Fourth Republic, from 1947 to 1954. A former finance minister under Léon Blum, he presided over the Constituent Assembly in 1946 and as president oversaw frequent changes of government in…

vincenzo-i-gonzaga.s: Vincenzo I Gonzaga was Duke of Mantua and of Montferrat from 1587 to 1612. A lavish patron of the arts, he employed Claudio Monteverdi and Peter Paul Rubens at his court, and in Montferrat he built the great citadel of Casale around 1590 to guard the duchy.

virbhadra-singh.s: Virbhadra Singh was the last Raja of the princely state of Bashahr in the western Himalaya and an Indian National Congress politician. After the state merged into India he served six terms as Chief Minister of Himachal Pradesh between 1983 and 2017, as well as a member of…

vishwanatha-nayak.s: Vishwanatha Nayak was the founder of the Madurai Nayak dynasty. Son of the Vijayanagara general Nagama Nayak, he was appointed governor of Madurai by the Vijayanagara Empire around 1529 after a rebellion there, and organised the region into palayams, military fiefs held by…

vistula-lagoon.s: The Vistula Lagoon is a brackish lagoon on the southern Baltic coast, separated from the Gulf of Gdańsk by the Vistula Spit and now divided between Poland and Russia. The Prussian lands of Pogesania and Warmia lay along its shores before the Teutonic conquest of the 13th century.

vladimir-the-bold.s: Vladimir the Bold, Prince of Serpukhov and Borovsk, was a cousin of Grand Prince Dmitry Donskoy of Moscow and his leading general. He commanded the reserve regiment that decided the Battle of Kulikovo against the Golden Horde in 1380, and he defended Moscow during Edigu's raid…

vladimir-the-great.s: Vladimir the Great was Grand Prince of Kiev from about 980 to 1015. In 988 he accepted Christianity from Byzantium and married the emperor's sister Anna, bringing churches, Church Slavonic writing and Byzantine art to Kievan Rus'.

vladimir-yaroslavich-of-galicia.s: Vladimir Yaroslavich was Prince of Galicia, son of Yaroslav Osmomysl. Driven out by his boyars and briefly ousted by Hungary in 1188, he regained Halych with the help of Frederick Barbarossa and Poland.

vladimir-yudovsky.s: Vladimir Yudovsky was a Bolshevik revolutionary in Odessa. In January 1918, after the Bolsheviks took the city, he became head of the council of people's commissars of the Odessa Soviet Republic, which claimed the city and its province until Austro-Hungarian and German troops…

vladislaus-ii-of-bohemia.s: Vladislaus II of Bohemia was Duke of Bohemia from 1140 and its second king from 1158, when Frederick Barbarossa raised him to royal rank for supporting the emperor's Italian campaigns. Barbarossa also granted him the land of Bautzen, beginning Upper Lusatia's long connection…

vladislav-ii-of-serbia.s: Vladislav II was the son of King Stefan Dragutin of Serbia, who ruled the northern lands later called the Kingdom of Syrmia. After Dragutin's death in 1316 his uncle King Stefan Milutin seized most of these lands and imprisoned him; later released, he claimed the Serbian…

vladko-macek.s: Vladko Maček was leader of the Croatian Peasant Party after the assassination of Stjepan Radić in 1928. Through the Cvetković–Maček Agreement of 1939 he secured the autonomous Banovina of Croatia within Yugoslavia and became deputy prime minister; he refused to collaborate…

vojislav-kostunica.s: Vojislav Koštunica is a Serbian lawyer and politician who defeated Slobodan Milošević in the Yugoslav presidential election of September 2000; Milošević's refusal to concede led to the protests of 5 October that overthrew him. Koštunica was President of the Federal Republic of…

volodymyr-shcherbytsky.s: Volodymyr Shcherbytsky was First Secretary of the Communist Party of Ukraine from 1972 to 1989 and a member of the Soviet Politburo. A close ally of Leonid Brezhnev, he replaced Petro Shelest, pursued Russification and repression of dissidents, and led Soviet Ukraine at the…

volodymyr-vynnychenko.s: Volodymyr Vynnychenko was a Ukrainian writer and Social Democratic politician. He headed the General Secretariat, the first government of the Ukrainian People's Republic, in 1917–1918, and in December 1918 led the Directorate with Symon Petliura that overthrew the Hetmanate…

volodymyr-zatonsky.s: Volodymyr Zatonsky was a Ukrainian Bolshevik and member of the People's Secretariat, the Soviet government formed in Kharkiv in December 1917 in opposition to the Ukrainian People's Republic. He later served as people's commissar of education in Soviet Ukraine and was executed…

vsevolod-mstislavich-of-belz.s: Vsevolod Mstislavich was a prince of the Volhynian branch of the Rurikids, a son of Mstislav II of Kiev and brother of Roman Mstislavich. In the later 12th century he ruled Belz as an appanage of Volhynia, making the town the seat of a small principality on the border with…

vukasin-mrnjavcevic.s: Vukašin Mrnjavčević was a Serbian noble crowned king in 1365 as co-ruler with Emperor Uroš V, ruling lands in western Macedonia from Prilep. With his brother Jovan Uglješa, despot of Serres, he led a Christian army against the Ottomans and was killed at the Battle of Maritsa…

vytautas-the-great.s: Vytautas the Great was Grand Duke of Lithuania from 1392 to 1430, son of Kęstutis of Trakai and cousin of Jogaila. He led Lithuanian forces with Poland to victory over the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald in 1410, extended the grand duchy towards the Black Sea, and settled…

vytautas-landsbergis.s: Vytautas Landsbergis is a Lithuanian musicologist and politician who led the Sąjūdis reform movement.
